title: India’s Carmakers Just Posted Their Best June Ever. Maruti Crossed 200,000 in a Single Month.
excerpt: Maruti Suzuki set an all-time monthly record, Mahindra’s sales surged 37%, and exports are booming — even as Europe’s automakers issue profit warnings and cut jobs.
body:
India’s automakers just wrapped up their strongest June on record, posting sales numbers that stand in sharp contrast to the profit warnings and production cuts cascading through European and American car companies.

Maruti Suzuki India Limited, the country’s largest carmaker, reported total sales of 200,390 units for June — an all-time monthly record. The tally combined 150,150 units sold domestically, 7,472 units supplied to other manufacturers, and a notable 42,768 units shipped for export. For a company that sold its first car — the Maruti 800 — in 1983, crossing 200,000 in a single month marks a milestone in India’s industrial story.

Mahindra & Mahindra posted an even more dramatic growth rate. Total automotive sales hit 1,06,207 vehicles, a 37% jump year-on-year. The utility vehicles segment — anchored by the XUV700, Thar, and Scorpio — grew 28% domestically, while total exports surged 125% compared to June 2025. Light commercial vehicles under 3.5 tonnes climbed 35%, and three-wheeler sales, including electric variants, grew 63%.

“The performance reflected broad-based demand traction across the product portfolio,” said Nalinikanth Gollagunta, CEO of Mahindra’s automotive division.

Hyundai Recovers, EVs Gain Ground

Hyundai Motor India Limited posted total sales of 51,335 units, a solid showing given that the company lost production days after a fire at a supplier’s facility earlier in June. The company said it resumed full operations by June 22 and expects to recover the lost output by the second quarter of FY2026-27.

The broader EV momentum is accelerating. Electric vehicle inquiries and bookings are up 15–20% month-on-month across the industry, driven by fuel cost concerns — crude oil spiked above $120 a barrel during the Iran-Hormuz crisis in April — and a wave of new electric models entering the market. Delhi’s new EV mandate, which bans the sale of new petrol two-wheelers from 2028, is adding urgency to the transition.

Auto stocks climbed on the Nifty on Wednesday. The auto index rose 1.2%, with Ashok Leyland gaining 2.8% and Mahindra & Mahindra up 2%.

The Export Story

What’s less visible in the monthly headline is the export surge. Indian automakers are increasingly competitive in markets across Africa, Latin America, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East. Mahindra’s 125% export jump is the sharpest example, but Maruti’s 42,768-unit export tally — more than many European marques sell domestically in a month — tells the same story from a different angle.

India exported roughly 680,000 passenger vehicles in FY2025-26, up from fewer than 400,000 five years earlier. The weak rupee, competitive manufacturing costs, and a new generation of models designed for global markets are driving the trend.

The European Counter-Signal

The Indian numbers land the same week that KPIT Technologies — an Indian auto-software firm that serves BMW, Volvo, and other European automakers — tumbled 17% after warning that several European clients had suddenly cut spending. “The slowdown was not anticipated earlier and has materialised recently,” KPIT’s management told investors.

European automakers are struggling with weak demand, surging Chinese competition, and the staggering cost of electrification. India’s domestic market, by contrast, is expanding on multiple fronts simultaneously: the ICE segment continues to grow on rising incomes and rural penetration, while EVs are adding a new layer of demand on top.

Why NRIs Should Watch

For the diaspora, the numbers carry investment implications. Maruti, Mahindra, and Tata Motors have been among the strongest performers on the Indian indices this year, and the June data reinforces the growth thesis. India’s auto sector — which contributes roughly 7% of GDP and employs over 35 million people directly and indirectly — is one of the most tangible bets on India’s domestic consumption story.

The contrast with the West is hard to ignore. While Ford, GM, and Stellantis shutter plants and negotiate buyouts, Indian manufacturers are adding capacity, launching new platforms, and shipping record volumes abroad. Suzuki is investing over $5 billion in a new EV battery and vehicle plant in Gujarat. Mahindra is building electric SUVs at a new facility in Pune. Tata is ramping its EV line across multiple models.

HSBC analysts expect consumer companies to post steady June-quarter growth, supported by resilient demand and selective price hikes. But they warned that El Niño conditions and a potentially weak monsoon could dampen rural demand later in fiscal 2027 — a risk worth monitoring for the sector’s mass-market segment.

For now, though, the numbers speak for themselves. June 2026 was the best month Indian carmakers have ever had.
